lower courts since Morrison have repeatedly held that Congress does not 
impermissibly undermine executive authority over prosecutions by 
authorizing c^ui tcrni actions, that is, prosecutions for violations of public 
statutes brought by private persons, even in cases when the executive has 
decided not to prosecute. Riley v, St, Liuke s Episcopal Hospital, 252 F.3d 
749 (5th Cir. 2001) (en banc) (upholding qui tarn provisions of the False 
Claims Act); United States ex rel. Stillwell v. Hughes Helicopters, Inc., 714 
F. Supp. 1084 (C.D. Cal. 1989) (same); United States ex rel. Truong v. 
Northrop Corp., 728 F. Supp. 615 (C.D. Cal. 1989) (same). See generally 
Note, The False Claims Act, Qui Tam Relators, and the Government, Which 
is the Real Party to the Action?, 43 STAN. L. Re v . 1061 (1991). In upholding 
qui tarn actions as consistent with Article III standing concerns, the 
Supreme Court purported to reserve the Article II issue. Vermont Agency 
of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765, z z8 n. 
8 (2000). Yet because the Court based its Article HI conclusion in large part 
on the history of qui tarn authorizations during the founding decades and 
because the same people wrote both Article II and Article III, it is not easy 
to see how history could support a different conclusion with regard to the 
executive power concern.
But this only teUs a part of the story of pluralism in federal policy 
implementation. The prospects for coordination have no doubt been 
reduced also by two critically important trends towards decentralization. 
The first is the federal government’s increasing reliance on state and local 
officials to implement federal regulatory goals. Although Congress is not 
constitutionally permitted to order state legislators to pass particular laws 
or to compel state administrators to enforce federal statutes. New York v. 
United States, 505 U.S. 144 (1992), it may induce cooperative state action 
by providing states some form of subsidy in exchange for state willingness 
to implement an administrative program under federal standards, Nat'l 
Fed^n of Independent Business v. Sebelius, 132 S. Ct. 2566 (2012). Such 
shared responsibility is especially prominent in the fields of social 
insurance (including Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security), 
transportation planning, education, health care, and environmental 
protection. Although federally funded state programs operate under some 
degree of federal supervision, committing the day-to-day pursuit of federal 
goals to government officials whose paychecks do not come from 
Washington, D.C. and who do not report in any plausible sense to the White 
House obviously has impheations for the “unitary executive” ideal.
